subject: maths
title: Data and Tally Marks: Sort, Count and Picture Graphs
seo_title: Year 1 Data and Tally Marks Worksheets: Sorting, Tally Marks and Picture Graphs (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
meta_desc: Free Year 1 maths worksheets on data for the Australian Curriculum (AC9M1ST01, AC9M1ST02): sort and count, read tally marks in bundles of 5, read picture graphs with one picture for each, find the most and fewest, and answer “how many more?”. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Sort it, count it, show it.
key_sub: A tally bundle is 5: count 5, 10, then count on the single marks. In a picture graph each picture is 1. How many more means compare; altogether means add.
body_html:
The big idea

Data is information we collect, like votes or things we count. First we sort things into groups. Then we count each group. Then we show the numbers with tally marks or a picture graph.

Sort and count

Put the same shapes together. Touch each one as you count it.

Tally marks: bundles of 5

Make one mark for each thing. The 5th mark goes across the first 4. That makes a bundle of 5. To read a tally, count the bundles by 5s, then count on the single marks.

Picture graph

In a picture graph, one picture stands for one thing. Put your finger on the name. Then count the pictures in that row only.

Most and fewest

The most is the biggest number. In a picture graph it is the longest row. The fewest (also called the least) is the smallest number.

Most and fewest

Apple 7, Banana 3, Mango 5. Which fruit got the most votes? Which got the fewest?

7 is the biggest number. 3 is the smallest number.

Answer: Most: Apple. Fewest: Banana

How many more?

How many more or how many fewer means compare. Match the pictures one to one, or take the smaller number away from the bigger one. Altogether means add.

How many more?

How many more votes did Apple get than Mango?

Apple 7, Mango 5. 2 stars are left over. 7 − 5 = 2.

Answer: 2 more votes

How many altogether?

How many votes were there altogether?

Apple 7, Banana 3, Mango 5. 7 + 3 + 5 = 15.

Answer: 15 votes

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting a bundle of tally marks as 4, or as 64 marks and 1 line across is 5
Reading the row above or belowPut your finger on the name first, then read that row
Counting a shape twice or skipping oneTouch or cross out each one as you count
Adding when it asks how many moreHow many more or fewer means compare, so subtract
Answering a name when it asks how manyHow many wants a number, like 4 votes
Counting the rows instead of the thingsAltogether means add the numbers in each row

faq.q: What do Year 1 students learn about data in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: They collect data by asking questions and record it with objects, drawings, lists and tally marks (AC9M1ST01). They show it in one-to-one displays such as picture graphs and talk about what it shows, like which group has the most (AC9M1ST02).

faq.q: How do you teach tally marks in Year 1?
faq.a: Make one mark for each thing, and draw the 5th mark across the first 4 to make a bundle of 5. To read a tally, count the bundles by 5s and then count on the single marks, so 1 bundle and 2 marks is 7.
It is a graph where one picture, object or square stands for one thing. A picture graph with one picture for each vote is a one-to-one display, so you can just count the pictures.

faq.q: How can I practise data with my Year 1 child at home?
faq.a: Ask the family a question, such as their favourite fruit, and keep a tally. Then ask “Which got the most?” and “How many more votes did apples get than bananas?”

sets.title: Which has the most? Which has the fewest?

items.q: Sort the shapes. Which shape is there the most of?
items.e: Sort and count. Circles: 3. Triangles: 5. Squares: 7. 7 is the biggest number, so there are the most squares.
Sort and count. Squares: 6. Stars: 5. Triangles: 3. 3 is the smallest number, so there are the fewest triangles.

items.q: Who read the most books?

items.q: We kept a weather chart for 2 weeks. How many more days were cloudy than windy?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Cloudy: 9. Windy: 4. Match them up one to one. 5 are left over: 9 − 4 = 5. The answer is 5 more days.

items.q: Students picked a game for recess. How many students picked the slide or skipping?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Slide: 7. Skipping: 6. Altogether means add: 7 + 6 = 13 students.

items.q: Some friends found shells at the beach. How many more shells did Mia find than Isla?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Mia: 8. Isla: 6. Match them up one to one. 2 are left over: 8 − 6 = 2. The answer is 2 more shells.

items.q: Some students told us about their pets. How many fewer students have a cat than a bird?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Bird: 9. Cat: 3. Match them up one to one. 6 are left over: 9 − 3 = 6. The answer is 6 fewer students.

items.q: Class 1B voted for a favourite fruit. How many votes were there altogether?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Banana: 4. Mango: 9. Orange: 6. Add all three: 4 + 9 + 6 = 19 votes. (There are 3 rows, but the answer is the number of votes.)

items.q: Students chose a snack for the class party. How many more students chose popcorn than yoghurt?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Popcorn: 8. Yoghurt: 2. Match them up one to one. 6 are left over: 8 − 2 = 6. The answer is 6 more students.

items.q: We asked how students get to school. How many students come by car or walk?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Car: 3. Walk: 2. Altogether means add: 3 + 2 = 5 students.

items.q: Year 1 voted for an ice-cream flavour. How many fewer votes did Lemon get than Mint?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Mint: 6. Lemon: 1. Match them up one to one. 5 are left over: 6 − 1 = 5. The answer is 5 fewer votes.

items.q: We counted birds in the park. How many more lorikeets than magpies did we see?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Lorikeet: 8. Magpie: 1. Match them up one to one. 7 are left over: 8 − 1 = 7. The answer is 7 more birds.

items.q: Class 1G voted for a favourite colour. How many more votes does Green need to have as many as Yellow?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Yellow: 11. Green: 2. Green needs to get from 2 up to 11. Count on from 2 to 11, or 11 − 2 = 9. So Green needs 9 more votes.

items.q: Year 1 voted for an ice-cream flavour. How many votes were there altogether?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Berry: 2. Mint: 6. Lemon: 5. Add all three: 2 + 6 + 5 = 13 votes. (There are 3 rows, but the answer is the number of votes.)

items.q: Some friends counted the books they read. How many more books did Ruby read than Zara?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Ruby: 12. Zara: 3. Match them up one to one. 9 are left over: 12 − 3 = 9. The answer is 9 more books.

items.q: Some friends found shells at the beach. How many fewer shells did Isla find than Jack?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Jack: 9. Isla: 3. Match them up one to one. 6 are left over: 9 − 3 = 6. The answer is 6 fewer shells.

items.q: Students chose a snack for the class party. How many students chose yoghurt or popcorn?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Yoghurt: 3. Popcorn: 9. Altogether means add: 3 + 9 = 12 students.

items.q: Class 1B voted for a favourite fruit. How many more votes does Apple need to have as many as Orange?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Orange: 9. Apple: 3. Apple needs to get from 3 up to 9. Count on from 3 to 9, or 9 − 3 = 6. So Apple needs 6 more votes.

items.q: Students picked a game for recess. How many more students picked tag than the slide?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Tag: 3. Slide: 1. Match them up one to one. 2 are left over: 3 − 1 = 2. The answer is 2 more students.

items.q: We sorted the toys in the box. How many fewer cars than balls are in the box?
items.e: Count the circles. Each one is 1. Balls: 7. Cars: 2. Match them up one to one. 5 are left over: 7 − 2 = 5. The answer is 5 fewer toys.

items.q: We asked how students get to school. How many students are shown altogether?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Car: 2. Walk: 12. Bike: 6. Add all three: 2 + 12 + 6 = 20 students. (There are 3 rows, but the answer is the number of students.)

items.q: Class 1G voted for a favourite colour. How many more votes does Red need to have as many as Blue?
items.e: Count the squares. Each one is 1. Blue: 8. Red: 6. Red needs to get from 6 up to 8. Count on from 6 to 8, or 8 − 6 = 2. So Red needs 2 more votes.

items.q: We counted birds in the park. How many more magpies than lorikeets did we see?
items.e: Count the tally marks. A bundle is 5. Magpie: 8. Lorikeet: 1. Match them up one to one. 7 are left over: 8 − 1 = 7. The answer is 7 more birds.
